did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a loud call to those appointed to punish the city: “Come near, you who are appointed over the city.” With them is a man carrying a weapon of destruction.

Did you know? Six men come from the direction of the upper gate facing north and stand beside the bronze altar. One of them is dressed in linen and carries a writing case at his waist, distinguishing him from the other bearers of destructive weapons.
Did you know? The glory of the God of Israel moves from above the cherub to the threshold of the temple. This movement takes place before the command to mark those who are to be protected.
Did you know? The man dressed in linen is commanded to go throughout Jerusalem and mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over all the detestable practices being committed in the city.

Did you know? The bearers of the destructive weapons are commanded to strike without mercy, but they are forbidden to approach anyone who bears the mark. In this way, the text distinguishes between those who bear the mark and the rest of the city’s inhabitants.
Did you know? The punishment begins in the temple itself: the command is, “Begin at my sanctuary,” and the first to be struck are the elders in front of the temple.

Did you know? After being commanded to defile the temple and fill the courtyards with the slain, the bearers of the destructive weapons leave the temple and strike the city. This description presents the spread of the destruction from the temple to Jerusalem.

Did you know? Ezekiel falls facedown and cries out, fearing that the LORD will destroy all the remnant of Israel. But the answer emphasizes the seriousness of the sin: the land is full of bloodshed and the city is full of injustice, while the people say that the LORD has abandoned the land and does not see.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the man dressed in linen returns and reports that he has done everything he was commanded to do. This concludes the vision of marking and destruction with a report that the task has been completed.
